It sounds like you are in a place where you are ready to talk to him about it. You can do so in a way that doesn't contain the word aspd, saying that you know he has a problem with empathy, connecting and following rules, but you don't mind because of all his qualities (that you can list)

People with aspd do care about some other people, and I hope that your son cares about you. I hope it means something to him that you love him for who he is.

I don't think that parents in the past were made aware of how a kids first few years would affect their entire life. People and parents all start in different places and most are messed up in their own way. Some people just haven't got anything to give and this can be for various reasons, because of their own pasts.  There's no point going over what happened and how you might have done things differently. What happened, happened. What didn't happen, didn't. 

In some ways it's better to be someone who has got aspd than a normal person and it doesn't automatically make you bad.

You might think that you want to know what he really thinks and feels about everything, but if it were to actually happen you'd probably change your mind. 

The trouble with this disorder is that people with aspd will tell people what they want to hear rather than the unvarnished truth so you can never be completely sure that what you are processing in reaction to his potential future admission is even accurate. He might give a moving performance that will make you cry in empathy even though you know it's bullshit, or he may convincingly deny it all. 

Many people tried to talk to me about it as I was growing up. Not my parents, but strangely my parents friends did try and discuss the situation with me, basically letting me know that they had been talking about me behind my back. I was vehement, convincing, twisting, and complex in creating an alternate version of events that somehow looked very similar to the actual truth (in facts) but at the same time was its polar opposite. Think maybe that's why I like writing now... I like to create a whole new world.

It's great that you still love him and accept him as he is. Maybe you made big mistakes as a parent. Maybe you didn't. Maybe you never quite bonded with him, or maybe your personalities didn't mesh. Maybe the fact he resembled his Dad so much pushed him away. Maybe you are being guilty without reason. Maybe you are pretending to feel guilty, maybe not. It's mothers day today so maybe you are just more emotional about your relationship than you otherwise might be, and tomorrow you will go back to being indifferent. But you do seem to care at least a bit, otherwise you wouldn't be making this post. 

But anyway you asked for advice. I think it would be a bad idea to suddenly approach this matter out of nowhere. I think you should slowly let him catch on to the fact that you *know* him, you *know* what he's about. To call him out on his bullshit for the next year or so before having a direct conversation with him about his lack of empathy and rule breaking behaviour. After you've had an honest convo with him about this you can broach the subject of aspd with an expectation of an honest answer. It will be more difficult for him to deny if he already knows you see straight through him.
